key_concepts: Significant figures represent the precision of a measurement
Rules: non-zero digits are significant, leading zeros are NOT, captive zeros ARE, trailing zeros after decimal ARE
In multiplication/division, result has same sig figs as least precise factor
In addition/subtraction, result has same decimal places as least precise term
examples: 0.0045 has 2 sig figs (leading zeros don't count)
2.50 has 3 sig figs (trailing zero after decimal counts)

key_concepts: Dimensions express physical quantities in terms of M, L, T
Principle of homogeneity: only quantities with same dimensions can be added/subtracted
Used to check equation correctness, derive relationships, convert units
Cannot determine dimensionless constants or add/subtract terms of different dimensions
examples: Dimension of G from F = GMm/r²: [M⁻¹L³T⁻²]

key_concepts: Triangle law: if two vectors are represented by two sides of triangle in order, resultant is third side
Parallelogram law: resultant is diagonal through common point
Polygon law: multiple vectors form closed polygon → resultant is closing side
Resultant magnitude and direction found using cosine and sine rules
formulas: If θ = 90°: R = √(A²+B²), tan α = B/A
examples: Two forces 3N and 4N at 90°: R = √(9+16) = 5N, tan α = 4/3, α = 53.1°
Three forces 3N, 4N, 5N forming closed triangle → resultant = 0 (equilibrium)

key_concepts: Any vector can be resolved into two perpendicular components
Components along x and y axes: A_x = A cos θ, A_y = A sin θ
Original vector: A = √(A_x² + A_y²), θ = tan⁻¹(A_y/A_x)
Unit vectors: î, ĵ, k̂ along x, y, z axes respectively
examples: Resolve 10N at 30°: A_x = 10 cos 30° = 8.66N, A_y = 10 sin 30° = 5N
Force 50N at 60° to horizontal: horizontal = 25N, vertical = 43.3N

key_concepts: Dot product (scalar product): A·B = AB cos θ, result is scalar
Cross product (vector product): A×B = AB sin θ n̂, result is vector perpendicular to both
Dot product gives work, power, flux
Cross product gives torque, angular momentum, magnetic force
formulas: A·B = AB cos θ = A_xB_x + A_yB_y + A_zB_z
A×B = AB sin θ n̂ (right-hand rule)
Work W = F·d = Fd cos θ

key_concepts: Projectile motion combines horizontal uniform motion with vertical uniformly accelerated motion
Horizontal velocity remains constant (no air resistance)
Vertical motion has constant acceleration g downward
Trajectory is a parabola
Time of flight, maximum height, and range are key parameters
formulas: T = 2u sin θ / g (time of flight)
Trajectory: y = x tan θ - gx²/(2u²cos²θ)
Time of flight for horizontal projection: T = √(2h/g)
examples: Two projectiles at θ and (90-θ) with same speed have same range

key_concepts: Centripetal acceleration always points toward center of circle
Centripetal force is not a new force — it's provided by tension, gravity, friction, etc.
Angular quantities: θ (rad), ω = dθ/dt, α = dω/dt
Relation: v = ωr, a_c = ω²r
examples: Car on curve r=50m, μ=0.5: max speed = √(μgr) = √(0.5×9.8×50) = 15.7 m/s
Conical pendulum: T cos θ = mg, T sin θ = mv²/r

key_concepts: Every particle attracts every other particle with force proportional to product of masses and inversely proportional to square of distance
Gravitational constant G = 6.674×10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg²
Gravitational force is always attractive, weakest fundamental force
Inside Earth, g decreases linearly with depth; outside, it follows inverse square law
examples: g at Earth's surface: g = 6.674×10⁻¹¹ × 5.97×10²⁴ / (6.371×10⁶)² = 9.81 m/s²
Escape velocity from Earth: v_e = √(2×9.81×6.371×10⁶) = 11.2 km/s
At height h=R: g' = g/4 = 2.45 m/s²

key_concepts: Force between two point charges is proportional to product of charges and inversely proportional to square of distance
Force acts along line joining charges, attractive for opposite, repulsive for same
Medium affects force: F = q₁q₂/(4πε₀εᵣr²)
Superposition principle: total force = vector sum of individual forces
Ohm's law: V = IR at constant temperature
Resistance depends on material (resistivity ρ), length L, area A
Series: R_eq = R₁+R₂+..., same current
Parallel: 1/R_eq = 1/R₁+1/R₂+..., same voltage
examples: Potentiometer: V = IR, potential gradient = V/L

key_concepts: Mass defect: difference between sum of individual nucleon masses and actual nuclear mass
Binding energy: energy equivalent of mass defect (E = Δmc²)
BE per nucleon curve: peaks at Fe-56 (most stable)
Nuclear fusion: light nuclei combine → energy released
Nuclear fission: heavy nucleus splits → energy released
examples: U-235 fission releases ~200 MeV per fission
Sun: 4H → He releases 26.7 MeV per reaction

key_concepts: Mole: amount of substance containing Avogadro's number of particles
Molar mass: mass of one mole of substance (g/mol)
At STP, 1 mole of any gas occupies 22.4 L
Molarity (M) = moles solute / liters solution
Molality (m) = moles solute / kg solvent
formulas: N = n × N_A (particles = moles × Avogadro's number)
examples: Volume of 2 mol O₂ at STP: V = 2×22.4 = 44.8 L
0.5M NaCl solution: 0.5 mol in 1L = 29.22g NaCl per liter

key_concepts: Four quantum numbers describe each electron uniquely
n (principal): energy level/shell (1, 2, 3, ...)
l (azimuthal): subshell shape (0 to n-1) → s,p,d,f
m_l (magnetic): orbital orientation (-l to +l)
m_s (spin): electron spin (+½ or -½)
examples: 3d orbital: n=3, l=2, m_l = -2,-1,0,+1,+2 (5 orbitals, 10 electrons)
4f orbital: n=4, l=3, m_l = -3 to +3 (7 orbitals, 14 electrons)

key_concepts: VSEPR: Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion theory
Electron pairs arrange to minimize repulsion
Order of repulsion: lp-lp > lp-bp > bp-bp
Steric number = bonding pairs + lone pairs
Determines molecular geometry and bond angles
formulas: Steric number = (valence electrons + monovalent atoms - charge)/2
examples: NH₃: SN=4 (3 bonds + 1 lp), trigonal pyramidal, 107°

key_concepts: IUPAC: International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry naming system
Identify longest carbon chain (parent)
Number chain to give substituents lowest numbers
Prefixes: mono-, di-, tri-, tetra- for multiples
Suffixes: -ane, -ene, -yne for saturation
formulas: Root: meth(1), eth(2), prop(3), but(4), pent(5), hex(6), hept(7), oct(8)

key_concepts: Cell theory: all organisms made of cells, cell is basic unit of life, all cells come from pre-existing cells
Prokaryotic cells: no nucleus, no membrane-bound organelles, smaller (1-10 μm)
Eukaryotic cells: true nucleus, membrane-bound organelles, larger (10-100 μm)
Animal cells lack cell wall, chloroplasts, large vacuole; have centrioles
Plant cells have cell wall (cellulose), chloroplasts, large central vacuole
formulas: Surface area to volume ratio limits cell size
examples: Human red blood cell: 7-8 μm, no nucleus
Plant palisade cell: has chloroplasts, cell wall

key_concepts: Mitosis: one division, produces 2 identical diploid cells (2n→2n)
Meiosis: two divisions, produces 4 non-identical haploid cells (2n→n)
Mitosis phases: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase
Meiosis I: homologous chromosomes separate (reduction division)
Meiosis II: sister chromatids separate (like mitosis)
Crossing over in prophase I increases genetic variation
formulas: Chromosome number: diploid (2n) = 46 in humans, haploid (n) = 23
examples: Human skin cell mitosis: 46 chromosomes → 2 cells with 46 each
Human gamete meiosis: 46 chromosomes → 4 sperm/egg with 23 each
Crossing over: exchange of genetic material between homologous chromosomes

key_concepts: Flower parts: sepals (calyx), petals (corolla), stamens (androecium), carpels (gynoecium)
Stamen: anther (pollen) + filament
Carpel: stigma + style + ovary (contains ovules)
Ovary develops into fruit, ovule develops into seed
Flower types: complete/incomplete, perfect/imperfect, hypogynous/perigynous/epigynous
examples: Rose: hypogynous (ovary superior), 5 sepals, 5 petals, numerous stamens
Sunflower: capitulum inflorescence (many small flowers in head)

key_concepts: Venn diagrams visually represent set relationships
Union (A∪B): all elements in A or B or both
Intersection (A∩B): elements common to both A and B
Complement (A'): elements not in A
De Morgan's laws: (A∪B)' = A'∩B' and (A∩B)' = A'∪B'
formulas: If A and B disjoint: n(A∪B) = n(A)+n(B)
examples: In a class of 50, 30 play cricket, 25 play football, 15 play both: only cricket = 15, only football = 10, neither = 10

key_concepts: Fundamental identity: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1
Dividing by cos²θ: tan²θ + 1 = sec²θ
Dividing by sin²θ: 1 + cot²θ = csc²θ
Compound angle formulas for sin(A±B) and cos(A±B)
Double angle: sin2θ = 2sinθcosθ, cos2θ = cos²θ-sin²θ
Inverse exists only if determinant ≠ 0 (non-singular matrix)
A × A⁻¹ = A⁻¹ × A = I (identity matrix)
For 2×2 matrix, swap diagonal elements, change sign of off-diagonal
Used to solve systems of linear equations: X = A⁻¹B
Chain rule: derivative of composite function f(g(x)) is f'(g(x))·g'(x)
Used for functions within functions
Implicit differentiation: differentiate both sides w.r.t. x, treat y as function of x
Logarithmic differentiation: take ln of both sides before differentiating
examples: d/dx[ln(sin x)] = (1/sin x)·cos x = cot x
